title: introduce kernel workspace pool and KV-shard lazy eviction to reduce peak GPU workspace
author: Ava Martinez
release_notes: Introduces a kernel workspace pooling allocator and a lazy-eviction sharding policy for KV cache that together lower peak GPU workspace requirements and smooth memory usage under continuous batching. No public API changes; rollout guarded by feature flag runtime.workspace_pool and kv.lazy_eviction. Metrics added: runtime.workspace.peak_bytes, kv.shard_evictions.
description:
Motivation: Large transformer workloads frequently hit transient peak workspace allocations driven by per-kernel scratch buffers and full-model KV residency during continuous batching. This leads to elevated reserved GPU memory or forced model downscaling. This PR attacks two orthogonal contributors: (1) kernel scratch/workspace fragmentation and repeated allocations across back-to-back kernel launches; (2) KV cache residency that keeps large contiguous GPU allocations even when batching patterns make parts of the KV set cold.

Summary: Add a device-local kernel workspace pool with size-classed slabs and a thin handle API so kernels can reuse preallocated workspace instead of malloc/free per-launch. Add a KV-shard manager that shards KV by logical token ranges and implements a lazy eviction policy: shards are placed in pinned CPU memory and only promoted back to GPU on first access. Integrate both with the continuous batching scheduler so that batch lifetime and reservation logic informs eviction/promote decisions and workspace sizing.

Design:
- Workspace pool: per-GPU arena with size classes (128B, 1KB, 4KB, 32KB, 512KB, 2MB). Kernels request a workspace handle (size request) and are returned a buffer from the matching slab. The pool exposes reserve/commit/release semantics compatible with existing kernel signatures. Pools fall back to the allocator when exhausted, but we emit metrics and can fail fast under strict-mode.
- Kernel integration: modified internal kernel launch wrappers to accept optional external_workspace_handle. For legacy kernels that don't pass handles, we still allocate as before. Only a small set of hot kernels (attention, rotary, matmul-accumulate) were updated to use the pool.
- KV shard manager: splits KV cache into N shards keyed by block token ranges (default N = number_of_sm_units * 2). Shards live in a tier: GPU -> pinned CPU -> disk (optional). Shards are lazily migrated to GPU when a request touches their range. Eviction policy is occupancy-aware: when continuous-batcher signals low expected occupancy, older shards are demoted to pinned CPU to free contiguous GPU workspace for kernels.
- Scheduler hooks: continuous-batcher now calls workspace_pool.reserve_for_batch(batch_id, expected_peak_workspace) at batch start and release_for_batch at completion. The scheduler uses historical occupancy to pre-emptively demote KV shards that are unlikely to be touched during the batch.

Implementation notes:
- New files: src/runtime/workspace_pool.{cc,h}, src/runtime/kv_shard_manager.{cc,h}, modified batcher/scheduler to call the new hooks. A small shim in include/runtime/kernel_launch.h to accept the workspace handle. Unit tests and perf harness under tests/perf were added.
- Feature flags: runtime.workspace_pool (false in global flags by default), kv.lazy_eviction (true). Flags are plumbed via runtime config and console toggle for gradual rollout.
- Observability: added metrics runtime.workspace.allocated_bytes, runtime.workspace.peak_bytes, runtime.workspace.alloc_failures, kv.shard_promotions, kv.shard_demotions, kv.shard_promotion_time_ms. Console exposes per-route workspace peaks.

Benchmarks (internal, NV A100 40GB, batcher sim load):
- Baseline (main): peak workspace 31.2 GB, end-to-end 99th p99 latency 78 ms, throughput 420 tok/s.
- This PR (workspace_pool + kv lazy): peak workspace 22.8 GB (-27%), p99 latency 81 ms (+3.8%), throughput 414 tok/s (-1.4%).
- When runtime.workspace_pool strict-mode enabled (fewer fallbacks): peak workspace 19.6 GB (-37%), p99 latency 85 ms (+8.9%), throughput 402 tok/s (-4.3%).

Compatibility and rollout: Kernel callers that rely on automatic allocation continue to work. We start by enabling the workspace pool for a few models (gpt-small family) and the batcher in canary. KV lazy eviction is default-on for hosted but off for Dedicated by policy until we validate fragmentation behavior on reserved clusters.

Risks: Promoting KV shards on hot access can spike short-term latency; mitigations include background prefetch heuristics and batching of promotions. Workspace pooling introduces allocation reuse bugs risk (use-after-free) — addressed by scoped handles and UAF detection in debug builds.

Testing: unit tests for allocator size classes, shard demotion/promotion, and scheduler integration. Integration perf tests added to tests/perf that simulate token-steady workloads and tail-latency probes. QA ran an incident-style soak for 72 hours on staged clusters.

Checklist:
- [x] Workspace pool allocator implemented and covered by unit tests
- [x] Hot kernels updated to accept workspace handles
- [x] KV shard manager with lazy demotion implemented
- [x] Scheduler hooks and batcher integration done
- [x] Metrics and console plumbing added
- [x] Performance regression and memory reduction benchmarks collected
- [x] Feature flags and rollout plan documented

See changed files for specifics and the perf doc in docs/perf/kv-lazy-evict.md for full numbers.
